one_liner: C extension pairing a gumbo-derived HTML5 tokenizer with a direct-to-libxml2 tree build; far faster than pure-Python html5lib.
what_it_does: Parses HTML5 (including malformed real-world markup) into a tree via a single function, html5_parser.parse(). Default output is an lxml (or lxml.html) Element built in C; it can also adapt the same parse into stdlib etree, minidom, or BeautifulSoup, and handles character-encoding sniffing (BOM, meta charset, chardet fallback) internally. Not a drop-in for lxml.html.fromstring's build/ABI story, but the returned tree is a normal lxml tree usable anywhere lxml is used.
how_it_is_fast: Tokenizes and builds a parse tree in C using a modified copy of Google's gumbo-parser (vendored under gumbo/), then walks that gumbo tree once and constructs a libxml2 document directly in C (src/as-libxml.c) via an explicit stack-based traversal, before handing the finished xmlDoc to lxml with etree.adopt_external_document. This skips the extra Python-object-construction pass that gumbo's own Python bindings and BeautifulSoup-based stacks require, and skips html5lib's pure-Python tokenizer/tree-builder entirely.
when_to_use: Already building on lxml/libxml2 in Python and need spec-correct HTML5 (not HTML4/XML) tokenization and tree construction
Parsing large HTML documents or a high volume of pages where html5lib or BeautifulSoup+html5lib throughput is the bottleneck
Need HTML5-correct namespace handling for embedded SVG/MathML, which html5lib handles poorly
Parsing messy or slightly-XHTML-flavored markup, using maybe_xhtml to tolerate self-closed elements
Desktop/batch app parsing lots of untrusted real-world HTML in bulk, e.g. an e-book/EPUB pipeline (its proving ground is calibre)
when_not_to_use: Already calling lxml.html.fromstring/libxml2 directly and don't need strict HTML5 algorithm compliance -- html5-parser is not shown to beat libxml2 itself; selectolax's benchmark measured it slower than lxml.html on real pages (16.10s vs 9.09s over 754 pages)

Environment can't build/ship a C extension, or uses PyPI's binary lxml wheel (static libxml2) -- html5-parser raises a RuntimeError at import on a libxml2 version mismatch unless lxml is installed with --no-binary
Need streaming or head-only parsing to skip a large <body> -- not supported (open feature request, issue #31)
Parsing adversarial/untrusted fragments through non-HTML fragment_context -- a MathML-integration-point fragment case caused infinite looping (issue #29); confirm the fix is in your pinned version
Non-lxml treebuilder output (etree/dom/soup) needed -- those re-walk the tree in Python and lose most of the C-vs-C speed advantage

integration.dependencies: lxml >= 3.8.0 (must be installed with --no-binary so it links dynamic libxml2), chardet (encoding-detection fallback), optional BeautifulSoup4 for treebuilder='soup'
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler; setup.py compiles with -std=c99 -O3 -Wall -Werror -pedantic-errors on Unix, /O2 on Windows (MSVC via a dedicated win-ci.py script)
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows -- CI runs three OSes and four compilers per the README; no documented CPU-architecture restriction
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: the output is a standard lxml Element like lxml.html.fromstring would give, but html5-parser and lxml must share the exact same dynamically-loaded libxml2 build, so a plain `pip install html5-parser` next to a normal binary lxml wheel fails at import

gotchas: Binary lxml wheels bundle a static libxml2; you must `pip install --no-binary lxml lxml` first or you get a RuntimeError citing mismatched LIBXML_VERSION at import
sanitize_names defaults to True, silently rewriting non-ASCII-safe tag/attribute names to keep the tree valid XML -- turn it off if strict HTML5 spec fidelity matters more than XML-safety
Only the lxml/lxml_html treebuilders are fast; etree, dom, and soup treebuilders are implemented in Python on top of the same parse and are correspondingly slower
A fragment-parsing edge case at MathML integration points could infinite-loop (issue #29, filed and since closed) -- worth confirming on your pinned version if you parse untrusted fragments
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick html5-parser when you specifically need HTML5-spec-correct parsing into a real lxml/libxml2 tree from Python and can accept lxml's --no-binary build constraint. If the goal is raw throughput against libxml2 itself rather than against html5lib, selectolax (Lexbor backend, ~3.8x faster than lxml.html directly in its own benchmark) or lexbor beat it outright.
verified_claims_summary: Author's own benchmark.py, a single run on his own machine with Python 3 (no CPU, OS, or compiler flags stated), parsed a 5.7MB HTML file 100x with html5-parser vs 10x for the others: 0.397s vs html5lib 13.906s (35x, the apples-to-apples lxml-tree/HTML5 comparison), BeautifulSoup+html5lib 12.683s (8x), and BeautifulSoup+lxml.html 3.826s (2x -- this margin reflects BeautifulSoup's own overhead, not libxml2 speed, since html5-parser was not benchmarked against lxml.html/libxml2 used directly).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-20) and used in production inside calibre despite a small following (706 stars); Apache-2.0 and a compact C codebase, but the requirement to build lxml against a matching dynamic libxml2 makes it harder to vendor cleanly than a header-only or wheel-friendly library.
